question: Orvin went to the store with just enough money to buy \(30\) balloons. When he arrived he discovered that the store had a special sale on balloons: buy \(1\) balloon at the regular price and get a second at \(\tfrac13\) off the regular price. What is the greatest number of balloons Orvin could buy?
solution:
Use the regular price of one balloon as one unit of money. Orvin then has 30 units. A discount of \(\tfrac13\) means the second balloon costs \(1-\tfrac13=\tfrac23\) unit, so a pair costs
\[
1+\frac23=\frac53\text{ units}.
\]
His budget buys
\[
30\div\frac53=18
\]
pairs, giving \(18\cdot2=36\) balloons and using all his money.

To prove this is the greatest possible number, consider 37 balloons. Each discounted balloon requires a regular-price balloon, so at most 18 of the 37 can be discounted. Their total cost is therefore at least
\[
19+18\left(\frac23\right)=31
\]
units, more than his budget. Any larger purchase contains a purchase of 37 balloons and cannot cost less. Thus the greatest number is \(\boxed{36}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
